meta.title: Who really said "There are hopes the bloom of whose beauty would be spoiled by the trammels of description"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Dickens. Ellen Pickering wrote it in The Merchant's Daughter (1836), page 298; an 1862 anthology credited "Dickens" and the error stuck.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are hopes the bloom of whose beauty would be spoiled by the trammels of description'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is Ellen Pickering's, from her 1836 novel The Merchant's Daughter, confirmed on page 298 of the scanned first edition. Dickens never wrote it.

answer.label: Not Charles Dickens — actually Ellen Pickering
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is Ellen Pickering’s, not Dickens’s. Lord Clanellon speaks it to Florence Lyle on page 298 of volume one of her novel The Merchant’s Daughter (London: Richard Bentley, 1836) — confirmed word for word in the scanned first edition. Dickens was first credited in Henry Southgate’s 1862 quotation anthology, and the error has travelled ever since.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt:
“No, indeed, Lord Clanellon! I am a poor, stupid creature, unable to understand the text of your poetical extravagance without explanatory notes.”

“There are hopes the bloom of whose beauty would be spoiled by the trammels of description: too lovely, too delicate, too sacred for words, they should be only known through the sympathy of hearts!”

Florence looked silent amaze, though a faint glow came on her cheek, perhaps from his fixed gaze and a flickering consciousness.
trail: 1836 — The line appears on page 298 of The Merchant’s Daughter, vol. 1, whose title page names no author at all: it reads only “by the author of ‘The Heiress,’ ‘Agnes Serle,’ &c.” Scanned first edition ↗
25 January 1850 — The Lincolnshire Chronicle reprints the passage in its “Varieties” column with no author named, cutting it loose from the novel. Quote Investigator ↗
1862 — Henry Southgate’s Many Thoughts of Many Minds prints it under the heading “HOPE—Beauty of” and signs it simply “Dickens.” Southgate’s compilation ↗

1884 — Edward Parsons Day’s Day’s Collacon welds Pickering’s sentence onto a genuine Dickens passage about budding hopes from Dombey and Son, crediting the merged text to Dickens. Quote Investigator ↗
source.excerptNote: Pickering’s 1836 text has no comma after “hopes” and a colon before “too lovely.” Southgate’s 1862 reprint inserted the comma, and most modern quote sites carry a semicolon — but the words themselves have not changed.

source.rightsNote: The Merchant’s Daughter was published by Richard Bentley in London in 1836, so the novel and this sentence have been in the public domain in the United States for well over a century. Ellen Pickering died in 1843, the text is English in the original, and no later translation or edition is involved.

author.name: Ellen Pickering
author.heading: Who was Ellen Pickering?
author.bio: Ellen Pickering was an English novelist who wrote sixteen three-volume novels for the circulating-library market between the mid-1820s and her death in 1843. She was popular and professionally successful in her lifetime — Nan Darrell (1839) was reprinted into the 1860s — but her books were published in the anonymous “by the author of” style of the period, and her name faded fast after she died of scarlet fever at Bath on 25 November 1843. Her best-known sentence has spent well over a century attributed to Charles Dickens.

misattribution.heading: Why Dickens gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the tidiest misattributions on record: a real sentence by a real novelist, lifted out of its novel by a newspaper, handed to a more famous name by a Victorian anthologist, and never given back.

items.why: Dickens never wrote it. The line belongs to Lord Clanellon in Ellen Pickering’s The Merchant’s Daughter (1836), volume one, page 298. The Dickens credit begins with Henry Southgate’s 1862 anthology Many Thoughts of Many Minds, which prints the passage under “HOPE—Beauty of” and signs it “Dickens” with no work named. Southgate, 1862 ↗

items.scope: The Dickens passage it was fused with
items.why: Dickens did write about hopes in floral terms — “It is when our budding hopes are nipped beyond recovery by some rough wind, that we are the most disposed to picture to ourselves what flowers they might have borne, if they had flourished” — but that is about hopes destroyed, not hopes too lovely to describe. Quote Investigator shows Day’s Collacon (1884) running the two passages together under Dickens’s name. Dombey and Son at Project Gutenberg ↗

The words are Pickering’s exactly; only the punctuation has drifted. Her 1836 text reads “There are hopes the bloom of whose beauty” with no comma, and closes on an exclamation mark. Southgate’s 1862 reprint added the comma after “hopes” and ended on a full stop, and most quote sites today substitute a semicolon for her colon. The 1836 text ↗

Pages crediting the line to Dickens name no book, chapter or letter — because there is none to name. An attribution with no work behind it is the standard signature of a quotation that has been passed hand to hand rather than read in place. Quote Investigator’s account ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Ellen Pickering’s, written for The Merchant’s Daughter in 1836 and printed on page 298 of volume one. Quote Investigator traced the Dickens credit to Henry Southgate in 1862, and the scanned first edition confirms the original. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: What it actually means
lead: Read as an aphorism about hope, the line sounds like philosophy. Read in place, it is a man dodging a question. Lord Clanellon has been talking in what Florence Lyle calls “poetical extravagance,” and when she asks him flatly to explain himself, this is his answer — a beautifully constructed refusal to say out loud that he is in love with her. Florence, unimpressed, replies that his meaning is still beyond her comprehension and suggests they send for someone “more versed in the sentimental.”

That courtship scene is exactly what the misattribution erases. Once The Lincolnshire Chronicle lifted the sentence into a filler column in 1850, it stopped being a character’s evasion and became a free-floating thought about hope — the shape a sentence has to take before an anthologist can file it under a subject heading and sign it with whichever famous name is nearest.
detailsBody: Ellen Pickering was not obscure in her own time. She began publishing around 1825, produced sixteen three-volume novels, and earned roughly £100 a year at her peak — a working professional in the circulating-library trade. Her most successful book, Nan Darrell (1839), was still being reprinted in the 1860s. She died of scarlet fever at Bath on 25 November 1843.

Two things made her easy to overwrite. Her novels appeared in the anonymous house style of the period — the 1836 title page of The Merchant’s Daughter credits only “the author of ‘The Heiress,’ ‘Agnes Serle,’ &c.” — so a sentence quoted out of it carried no name to lose. And by the time Southgate’s anthology assigned it to Dickens in 1862, Pickering had been dead nearly twenty years, with no estate and no reputation to object.

The Dictionary of National Biography’s judgement on her has held: she enjoyed real success among her contemporaries and achieved no lasting legacy. This sentence is the one piece of her work most people have read — under someone else’s name.
context.pull: “Too lovely, too delicate, too sacred for words” — a man declining to say he is in love.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the line originated with Ellen Pickering in her 1836 novel The Merchant's Daughter (vol. 1, ch. 9, p. 298), spoken by Lord Clanellon to Florence Lyle; 1836 is the earliest known appearance. It documents the Lincolnshire Chronicle printing it unattributed in its Varieties column on 25 January 1850 (p. 7, col. 6), Henry Southgate's Many Thoughts of Many Minds (1862, p. 292) crediting Dickens, and Day's Collacon (1884, p. 385) merging it with a Dombey and Son passage under Dickens's name.

The Internet Archive scan of The Merchant's Daughter vol. 1 (Ellen Pickering, R. Bentley, London, 1836, 3 vols.) contains the exact sentence on page 298 in chapter IX: 'There are hopes the bloom of whose beauty would be spoiled by the trammels of description: too lovely, too delicate, too sacred for words, they should be only known through the sympathy of hearts!' spoken by Lord Clanellon to Florence. Its title page reads 'BY THE AUTHOR OF THE HEIRESS, AGNES SERLE, &c.' with no author name, imprint 'LONDON: RICHARD BENTLEY, NEW BURLINGTON STREET. 1836.'
Henry Southgate's Many Thoughts of Many Minds (1862) prints the passage under the subject heading 'HOPE—Beauty of' with a comma added after 'hopes', and signs it 'Dickens' with no work named.

Project Gutenberg's Dombey and Son by Charles Dickens (originally published in monthly installments 1846-1848) contains, in chapter 10, 'It is when our budding hopes are nipped beyond recovery by some rough wind, that we are the most disposed to picture to ourselves what flowers they might have borne, if they had flourished' — a passage about hopes destroyed, not hopes too lovely to describe.

The Dictionary of National Biography entry on Ellen Pickering records that she died of scarlet fever at Bath on 25 November 1843, began novel-writing around 1825, earned about £100 a year at her peak, and lists The Merchant's Daughter (1836) among her novels.

Wikipedia records Ellen Pickering (1802 – 25 November 1843) as a British novelist who published sixteen three-volume novels, notes Nan Darrell (1839) was reprinted five times through 1865, and states she 'enjoyed success among her contemporaries but achieved no lasting legacy'.
The At the Circulating Library database records Ellen Pickering and lists 'The Merchant's Daughter. 3 vol. London: Bentley, 1836.'
Quotefancy credits the quotation 'There are hopes, the bloom of whose beauty would be spoiled by the trammels of description; too lovely, too delicate...' to Charles Dickens and names no source work.
Wikisource's author page for Ellen Pickering (1802–1843, British novelist) lists The Merchant's Daughter (1836) with links to all three volumes.
